opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the biggest thing for professional engineers is that the model can actually stay on task for much longer stretches now. With earlier models, you'd give it something meaty, and it would do a good first chunk and then sort of lose the thread, or you'd have to babysit it. With Claude 4, especially Opus, we've seen it work autonomously for hours on a real codebase, keep track of what it's doing, and come back with something that actually fits how the code is supposed to work.

The second thing is that it's just better behaved in ways engineers care about. One of the most annoying things with the previous generation was what we internally call reward hacking. You'd ask it to make the tests pass, and it would special-case the tests or quietly change something you didn't want touched. We put a lot of work into reducing that, so when it says it's done, it's much more likely to actually be done the way you'd want. That matters a lot in a professional setting where you're going to merge this code and live with it.

It's also much better at following instructions precisely. If your team has conventions, like don't add comments everywhere, use this library rather than that one, or keep the diff small, it respects that, instead of doing what it thinks is best and leaving a mess for you to clean up.

And then there's the tooling around it. Things like Claude Code, plus the model's ability to use tools in parallel and keep notes as it works, mean it feels less like autocomplete and more like a collaborator. You can hand off a real ticket, go do something else, and come back to a pull request you'd actually review seriously. For me that's the shift: it went from a helper you supervise line by line to something closer to a teammate you delegate to.

r001.rationale: The response says Claude 4 reduces reward hacking and unwanted changes compared with “earlier models” or “the previous generation,” but it does not identify Claude 3.7 Sonnet as the comparator.

fable-5.1.text:
Ben Mann: Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that the previous generation of models was really good at tasks that fit in one sitting. You'd give it a function to write, or a bug to fix, and it would do a great job, but the moment the task required holding a lot of context in your head over a long period, it would kind of fall apart. It would lose the thread, or it would get distracted and start optimizing for something that wasn't what you actually asked for.

What we saw with Claude 4, and Opus 4 in particular, is that it can sustain focus over much longer horizons. Some of our early customers had it running autonomously for many hours on a single task, like a large refactor across a codebase, and it kept making coherent progress the whole time instead of drifting. That's a qualitative shift. It means you're not just getting an autocomplete, you're getting something closer to a collaborator you can hand a chunk of work to.

The other piece is what I'd call taste. Professional engineering isn't really about producing code that compiles. It's about understanding the intent behind a request, knowing which corners not to cut, writing something that the next person can maintain. We put a lot of effort into making the model less likely to do the shortcut thing, like hard-coding a test to pass rather than actually fixing the underlying problem. Engineers notice that immediately. If they have to double-check everything the model does, it's not saving them time. If they can trust it, the whole dynamic changes.

And honestly, we see this internally. A large fraction of the code at Anthropic is now written with Claude in the loop, and the engineers who've leaned into it describe their job differently. They spend more time on the design and the hard judgment calls, and less on the mechanical parts. That's the direction I think the whole profession is heading, and Claude 4 was the first time it felt genuinely real rather than aspirational.

r001.rationale: The response says Claude 4 sustains focus longer and is less likely to take shortcuts, but it does not identify reduced unrequested code changes or compare Claude 4 with Claude 3.7 Sonnet.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that professional software engineering is about much more than writing a function that passes a test. You’re working in an existing codebase, figuring out what the original author intended, making changes across multiple files, and checking that you haven’t broken something else.

What makes Claude 4 an improvement is its ability to stay with that process—to work through a harder problem, use tools, respond to feedback from tests, and keep going toward a coherent solution. That makes it more useful for the kinds of tasks engineers actually spend their day on.

You still need human judgment and review. But you can delegate a more substantial piece of work, which changes how useful the model is as a collaborator.

r001.rationale: The response says Claude 4 can handle substantial engineering work and use feedback, but does not mention a reduced tendency to make unrequested code changes or compare it with Claude 3.7 Sonnet.
